title: Bernoulli's Theorem and its Applications
short_intro: Bernoulli's theorem is a statement of the law of conservation of energy for flowing fluids, relating pressure, velocity, and elevation. It applies to streamline, steady, non-viscous, and incompressible fluid flows.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding the equation of continuity, conservation of energy basis, definition of static, dynamic, and hydrostatic pressure, Venturi meter, and Torricelli's law.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous work-energy derivation for fluid elements, generalizations for non-steady and compressible flows, Euler's equation of motion, and Magnus effect.

concept_notes.heading: Conservation of Energy Basis
bullets: Bernoulli's theorem is derived directly from the work-energy theorem applied to a continuous volume of fluid.
The total mechanical energy per unit volume (or mass) remains constant along any streamline in the absence of dissipative viscous forces.
It involves three energy terms per unit volume: pressure energy, kinetic energy, and potential energy.

concept_notes.heading: Pressure Heads in Fluid Flow
bullets: Static pressure head represents the potential energy stored in the fluid due to compressive forces per unit weight.
Velocity head or dynamic pressure represents the kinetic energy per unit weight of the flowing fluid.
Elevation head represents the potential energy per unit weight due to the gravitational field.

concept_notes.heading: Venturi Meter Operation
bullets: A Venturi meter measures the rate of flow of an incompressible fluid through a pipe using Bernoulli's principle.
At the constriction, the cross-sectional area decreases, causing the fluid velocity to increase and the static pressure to drop.
The pressure difference between the main section and the throat is measured using a differential manometer.

concept_notes.heading: Torricelli's Law of Efflux
bullets: Torricelli's theorem states that the velocity of efflux of a liquid through an orifice at a depth h below the free surface is equal to the velocity of a body falling freely through height h.
Derived by applying Bernoulli's equation between the open top surface of the liquid and the small orifice.
Assumes the cross-sectional area of the container is much larger than the area of the orifice.

derivations.title: Derivation of Bernoulli's Equation via Work-Energy Theorem
derivations.conditions: Ideal fluid, steady flow, streamline motion, incompressibility, non-viscous.
steps: Consider a fluid element of mass m entering a pipe of varying cross-section and height between cross-section A<sub>1</sub> (at height z<sub>1</sub>, pressure P<sub>1</sub>, speed v<sub>1</sub>) and A<sub>2</sub> (at height z<sub>2</sub>, pressure P<sub>2</sub>, speed v<sub>2</sub>) in time dt.
Work done by the pressure force at the inlet is W<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>1</sub> A<sub>1</sub> v<sub>1</sub> dt = P<sub>1</sub> V, where V is the volume of fluid passing per second.
Work done by the pressure force at the outlet is W<sub>2</sub> = -P<sub>2</sub> A<sub>2</sub> v<sub>2</sub> dt = -P<sub>2</sub> V.
Net work done by pressure forces in time dt is W_{net} = (P<sub>1</sub> - P<sub>2</sub>) V.
Change in potential energy of the fluid element is Delta U = mg(z<sub>2</sub> - z<sub>1</sub>) = rho V g (z<sub>2</sub> - z<sub>1</sub>).
Change in kinetic energy of the fluid element is Delta K = (1/2) m v<sub>2</sub>^2 - (1/2) m v<sub>1</sub>^2 = (1/2) rho V (v<sub>2</sub>^2 - v<sub>1</sub>^2).

Equating net work done to the total change in mechanical energy (W<sub>net</sub> = Delta U + Delta K): (P<sub>1</sub> - P<sub>2</sub>)V = rho V g (z<sub>2</sub> - z<sub>1</sub>) + (1/2) rho V (v<sub>2</sub>^2 - v<sub>1</sub>^2).
Dividing by volume V and rearranging yields the standard Bernoulli form.

derivations.title: Derivation of Venturi Meter Flow Rate Formula
derivations.conditions: Horizontal pipe (z<sub>1</sub> = z<sub>2</sub>), ideal fluid flow.
steps: Apply the equation of continuity between the inlet (area A<sub>1</sub>, speed v<sub>1</sub>) and the throat (area A<sub>2</sub>, speed v<sub>2</sub>): A<sub>1</sub> v<sub>1</sub> = A_{2} v<sub>2</sub>, which gives v<sub>1</sub> = (A<sub>2</sub> / A<sub>1</sub>) v<sub>2</sub>.
Apply Bernoulli's equation for horizontal flow (z<sub>1</sub> = z<sub>2</sub>): P<sub>1</sub> + (1/2) ho v<sub>1</sub>^2 = P<sub>2</sub> + (1/2) ho v<sub>2</sub>^2.
Express the pressure difference Delta P = P<sub>1</sub> - P<sub>2</sub> as Delta P = (1/2) ho (v<sub>2</sub>^2 - v<sub>1</sub>^2).
Substitute v<sub>1</sub> into the pressure difference equation: Delta P = (1/2) ho v<sub>2</sub>^2 [1 - (A<sub>2</sub> / A<sub>1</sub>)^2].
Solve for velocity at the throat v<sub>2</sub> and compute volume flow rate Q = A<sub>2</sub> v<sub>2</sub>.

formula_sheet.name: Bernoulli's Equation (Pressure Form)
formula_sheet.equation_html: P +  rac{1}{2}ho v^{2} + ho g z = 	ext{Constant}
formula_sheet.variables: P = static pressure, ho = density, v = flow speed, g = acceleration due to gravity, z = vertical height

formula_sheet.name: Bernoulli's Equation (Head Form)
formula_sheet.equation_html: rac{P}{ho g} +  rac{v^{2}}{2g} + z = 	ext{Constant}
formula_sheet.variables: P/(ho g) = pressure head, v<sup>2</sup>/(2g) = velocity head, z = elevation head
formula_sheet.conditions: Constant density fluid in a gravitational field

graphs_and_experiments.title: Venturi Tube Pressure Variation Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of pipe diameter and static pressure P along the horizontal coordinate x of a converging-diverging pipe.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Static pressure drops to a minimum value at the narrowest throat section where velocity is maximum, recovering partially as the pipe widens again.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in conceptual questions involving pressure-velocity trade-offs in conduits.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Prandtl-Pitot Tube Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic of an L-shaped tube pointing upstream into a flow with stagnation point at the tip and static holes on the side.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Measures total pressure (stagnation pressure) and static pressure simultaneously, allowing calculation of flow velocity via v = sqrt(2(P<sub>0</sub> - P)/rho).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to frame numerical and theoretical questions on fluid speed measurement.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Efflux Velocity vs. Depth (Torricelli's Law)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic or square-root curve showing efflux velocity v increasing with depth h.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that velocity is proportional to the square root of the head h, mirroring free fall kinematics.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via graphical interpretation questions in PGT examinations.

solved_numericals.question: Water flows through a horizontal pipe whose internal diameter is 4 cm at one end and 2 cm at the other end. If the speed of water at the wider end is 2 m/s, find the speed of water at the narrower end.
solution_steps: Use the equation of continuity: A<sub>1</sub> v<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub> v<sub>2</sub>.
Since area is proportional to the square of diameter (A = pi d^2 / 4), (d<sub>1</sub>^2) v<sub>1</sub> = (d<sub>2</sub>^2) v<sub>2</sub>.
Substitute values: (4 cm)^2 * (2 m/s) = (2 cm)^2 * v<sub>2</sub>.

solved_numericals.question: A cylindrical tank of height 5 m is filled with water. A small hole is punched at a depth of 1.25 m from the free surface. Find the velocity of efflux of water.
solution_steps: Given depth h = 1.25 m and g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

solved_numericals.question: Water flows through a horizontal Venturi meter with inlet and throat cross-sectional areas of 20 cm<sup>2</sup> and 10 cm<sup>2</sup> respectively. The pressure difference between the inlet and throat is 3 kPa. Calculate the volume flow rate of water (density of water = 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>).
solution_steps: Given A<sub>1</sub> = 20 cm<sup>2</sup> = 20 * 10<sup>-4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, A<sub>2</sub> = 10 cm<sup>2</sup> = 10 * 10<sup>-4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>.
Pressure difference Delta P = 3000 Pa, rho = 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>.
Use Venturi flow rate formula: Q = A<sub>1</sub> A<sub>2</sub> sqrt{ rac{2 Delta P}{ho (A_1^2 - A_2^2)}}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes fluid is completely incompressible (ho = constant), which fails for high-speed gases where compressibility effects dominate.
Assumes zero viscosity (non-viscous fluid); real fluids experience internal friction and viscous dissipation of mechanical energy into heat.
Restricted to steady flow where fluid properties at any point do not change with time.
Valid along a single streamline; applying it across different streamlines requires irrotational flow conditions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Bernoulli's theorem implies that fluid velocity causes pressure reduction directly without energy conservation.
common_misconceptions.correct: Pressure drop and velocity increase are alternate manifestations of mechanical energy conservation along a streamline.
common_misconceptions.why: Work done by pressure forces accelerates the fluid element, changing its kinetic and potential energy.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Equal transit time fallacy: air particles taking upper and lower paths around an aerofoil must meet at the trailing edge.
common_misconceptions.correct: Air passing over the curved upper surface of an aerofoil moves significantly faster than required by the equal transit time hypothesis.
common_misconceptions.why: Experimental observations show air over the top surface arrives at the trailing edge much earlier than air from the bottom surface.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Bernoulli's equation can be applied freely between any two arbitrary points in a turbulent or swirling viscous fluid.
common_misconceptions.correct: It holds strictly only along a streamline for steady, non-viscous, incompressible, irrotational flow.
common_misconceptions.why: Viscous shear stresses and turbulence cause mechanical energy to dissipate, violating the constant total energy condition.

quick_revision: Bernoulli's theorem is the conservation of mechanical energy applied to ideal fluid flow along a streamline.
Bernoulli's Equation (Pressure Form): P +  rac{1}{2}ho v^{2} + ho g z = 	ext{Constant}
Bernoulli's Equation (Head Form):  rac{P}{ho g} +  rac{v^{2}}{2g} + z = 	ext{Constant}
